Environmental Monitoring of a Dry-Blend Powder Line

S. Kleshchev1, L. Boyd1,2   1Quality Assurance, BlendHouse Portland   2Food Safety Mentor Program
Abstract. We review twelve months of environmental swabs from a dry-blend powder line. Zone 1 contact surfaces stayed below action limits in every month, while Zone 3 floor drains drove most presumptive positives. Sanitation after wet cleaning, not the blend recipe, explained the seasonal peak. We propose a risk-weighted sampling rotation and report the effect of the change on detection rates.

1 Introduction

Dry powder facilities depend on keeping water out. When water enters during a wet clean, organisms that persist in dry niches can grow, and a single harborage site can seed a whole zone3. Environmental monitoring (EM) programs therefore sample by zone, from product-contact surfaces (Zone 1) outward to non-production areas (Zone 4).

This report has three aims:

  • Describe positives by zone, site type and month.
  • Test whether wet cleaning predicts the next positive.
  • Propose a rotation that weights high-risk sites.

2 Methods

2.1 Sampling

Sites were swabbed with pre-moistened sponges over 100 cm2 where the surface allowed, otherwise the whole accessible surface. Each sample was enriched and screened for Salmonella spp. and Cronobacter spp. Presumptive positives were confirmed by the contract laboratory.

2.2 Risk score

Each site received a risk score from its zone weight wz, its moisture exposure m and its history of positives h:

R=wz·(1+m)+2h

Sites with R ≥ 6 were sampled weekly; the rest rotated monthly. A sampling plan of 1. weekly, 2. monthly and 3. quarterly tiers was kept.

  1. Weekly: all Zone 1 sites and any site with R ≥ 6.
  2. Monthly: remaining Zone 2 and Zone 3 sites.
  3. Quarterly: Zone 4.

3 Results

Across 1,284 swabs, 41 were presumptive positive and 17 confirmed. Zone 3 drains accounted for 11 of the 17 confirmed results. No Zone 1 site was confirmed positive. The monthly pattern (Figure 1) peaks in March and August, the two months with the most wet cleans.

Confirmed positives followed a wet clean within seven days in 13 of 17 cases (76%). A post-clean dry-out step, added in May, reduced that share to 2 of 6 in the second half of the year.

4 Discussion

The data point to water, not the blend recipe, as the driver. Drains and the floor around them stay wet for hours after a clean, and traffic carries that water toward Zone 2. The dry-out step shortened that window. A risk-weighted rotation puts more swabs where water lingers without adding total samples.

Two limits apply. Twelve months is short for seasonal claims, and the contract laboratory changed its enrichment method in October, which may shift detection.

5 Conclusion

Keep Zone 1 weekly. Move drains to weekly after any wet clean. Keep the dry-out step. Review the rotation after the next twelve months.

3 A harborage site is a niche where organisms survive cleaning, such as a cracked seal or a hollow roller.
